lessons.title: Sound recognition: consonant clusters and contracted forms
lessons.objective: Pronounce consonant clusters, distinguish sounds and use contracted forms in rapid speech.
lessons.course:
Consonant clusters are two or three consonants together: str (street, strong), spr (spray), pl (plate), cl (clinic), tr (treat), sk (skin). We pronounce every consonant without adding a vowel: “street”, not “sitreet”.
Contracted forms join two words with an apostrophe: I am → I’m, do not → don’t, it is → it’s, we will → we’ll, he has not → he hasn’t.
lessons.model: The adult says slowly, then fast: “The strong nurse sprays the clinic.” “I’m fine, but I don’t feel strong.”
lessons.guided: Say ten words with clusters, slowly then quickly. Turn five sentences into contracted forms.
lessons.exercise: What is the contracted form of “do not”?
lessons.remediation: Tap the consonants on the table as you say them.
lessons.transfer: Use three contracted forms when you talk at home.

practice.prompt: Match the full form and the contracted form.
Which word begins with a three-consonant cluster?
Listen and repeat quickly.
practice.listen: The strong nurse sprays the clinic. I’m fine, but I don’t feel strong.

lessons.title: Reading silently: a visit to the district hospital
lessons.objective: Read a text silently and answer questions about it.
lessons.course: Before reading, look at the title and guess what the text is about. Read the questions, then read silently. Find the sentence that answers each question.

support.title: Read silently
support.text: On Monday, Bih had a high fever. Her mother took her to the district hospital. They waited in the queue until a nurse called them. The nurse took Bih’s temperature: 39 °C. The doctor examined her and asked for a blood test. It was malaria. Bih received tablets and was told to sleep under a treated net. Three days later, she was back at school.

lessons.model: The adult reads the title, guesses aloud, then reads the questions and finds the first answer.
lessons.guided: Read the questions, then the text silently. Answer in full sentences.
lessons.remediation: Find the answers by underlining key words in the text.
lessons.transfer: Tell your family what to do when someone has a fever.

practice.prompt: What was Bih’s temperature?
Put the events in order.
items: The doctor asked for a blood test.

practice.prompt: After how many days was Bih back at school?

lessons.title: Dictation: the apostrophe s’ for many owners
lessons.objective: Use s’ for plural owners and write dictated sentences and a paragraph correctly.
lessons.course:
When the owners are plural and end in s, we add only an apostrophe: the nurses’ room (the room of the nurses), the doctors’ meeting, the patients’ beds. Irregular plurals take ’s: the children’s ward, the women’s clinic.
In a dictation: listen to the whole sentence first, write, then reread to check spelling and punctuation.
lessons.model: The adult dictates: “The nurses’ room is next to the children’s ward.” and shows the two apostrophes.
lessons.guided: Write a dictation of four sentences about a health centre. Check each apostrophe.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite: the room of the nurses.
lessons.remediation: First decide: one owner (’s) or many owners (s’)?
lessons.transfer: Write three phrases about your family with s’ or ’s.

practice.prompt: One owner or many? Choose.
Complete.
practice.text: the doctors[[’|']] cars; the children[[’s|'s]] toys

practice.prompt: Listen and write the dictation.
practice.listen: The nurses’ room is clean. The children’s ward is on the left. Visitors wash their hands at the door.

lessons.title: Pronouns: subject, object, possessive and relative
lessons.objective: Identify and use subject, object, possessive and relative pronouns in sentences.
lessons.course:
Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
Relative pronouns join two ideas: who (people), which (things), that (people or things), whose (owner). “The nurse who helped me is kind.” “The tablets which I took were bitter.”
lessons.model: The adult says: “This is the doctor. He treated me.” → “This is the doctor who treated me.”
lessons.guided: Replace nouns with pronouns in five sentences. Join four pairs of sentences with who or which.
lessons.exercise: Join: I saw the nurse. She vaccinated the baby.
lessons.answer: I saw the nurse who vaccinated the baby.
accept: I saw the nurse who vaccinated the baby
I saw the nurse that vaccinated the baby
lessons.remediation: Use who for people and which for things.
lessons.transfer: Describe three people you know using “who”.

practice.prompt: Match each subject pronoun with its object pronoun.
practice.explanation: Object pronouns come after the verb.

practice.prompt: Complete with who or which.
practice.text: The boy [[who]] fell is better. The medicine [[which]] he took is strong.
practice.explanation: who for people; which for things.

practice.prompt: This bag is my bag. It is …

lessons.title: Proper, improper and mixed fractions: sharing medicine and food
lessons.objective: Identify proper and improper fractions and mixed numbers and convert between them.
lessons.course:
Proper fraction: the numerator is smaller than the denominator: ¾, 2/5. Improper fraction: the numerator is bigger or equal: 7/4, 5/5.
Mixed number: a whole number and a fraction: 1¾. 7/4 = 1¾ because 4/4 = 1 whole and ¾ is left. 2½ = 5/2.
lessons.model: The adult cuts 2 loaves into quarters and gives 7 quarters: 7/4 = 1 whole loaf and ¾.
lessons.guided: Use paper circles to show 5/3, 9/4 and 3/2. Write each as a mixed number.
lessons.remediation: Shade the shapes, count the wholes, then the parts left.
lessons.transfer: Describe a meal shared in your family with fractions.

practice.prompt: Which fraction is improper?
3½ = ?/2. Write the numerator.
Match each fraction with its kind.

lessons.title: Mass: grams and kilograms at the health centre
lessons.objective: Establish the relationship between g and kg and convert and compare masses.
lessons.course:
1 kg = 1 000 g. Half a kilogram = 500 g; a quarter = 250 g.
At the health centre, babies are weighed in kg: 4 kg 300 g = 4 300 g. To compare masses, write them in the same unit.
lessons.model: The adult reads a baby scale: “The baby weighs 5 kg 200 g, that is 5 200 g.”
lessons.guided: Read the mass on five food packets. Convert each into g or kg and g. Order them from lightest to heaviest.
lessons.exercise: How many grams are there in 3 kg?
lessons.remediation: Use a scale and 1 kg packets to compare.
lessons.transfer: Read the mass on packets in your kitchen.

practice.prompt: A baby weighed 3 kg 500 g at birth and 5 kg 100 g at two months. How many grams did the baby gain?
Which is heavier?
How many 250 g packets make 1 kg?

lessons.title: Area of rectangles and squares: the floor of a clinic room
lessons.objective: Calculate the area of rectangles and squares in square units.
lessons.course:
The area is the space covered by a shape. We count squares or use a formula. Rectangle: A = length × width. Square: A = side × side.
A room 5 m long and 4 m wide has an area of 20 m² (square metres).
lessons.model: The adult draws a rectangle on squared paper, counts the squares, then multiplies length × width.
lessons.guided: Draw five rectangles on squared paper and find their area by counting, then with the formula.
lessons.exercise: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its area?
lessons.remediation: Count the squares row by row.
lessons.transfer: Estimate the area of your bedroom floor in square metres.

practice.prompt: A square tile has sides of 6 cm. Area in cm²?
Which unit measures area?
A room has an area of 24 m² and a width of 4 m. What is its length, in m?

lessons.title: Ranking data: heights and masses of pupils
lessons.objective: Arrange data in ascending and descending order and find the greatest and the smallest.
lessons.course:
Ascending order goes from the smallest to the greatest; descending order goes from the greatest to the smallest.
Heights in cm: 128, 135, 122, 140 → ascending: 122, 128, 135, 140. The range is greatest − smallest = 18 cm.
lessons.model: The adult measures four children and writes their heights, then ranks them.
lessons.guided: Measure the heights of five family members. Rank them in ascending and descending order. Find the difference between the tallest and the shortest.
lessons.remediation: Find the smallest first, cross it out, then find the next.
lessons.transfer: Rank your family members by age.

practice.prompt: Put the masses in descending order.
practice.explanation: From the greatest to the smallest.

practice.prompt: Heights: 140, 122, 135 cm. Difference between the tallest and the shortest, in cm?
Ascending order means…

lessons.title: Drugs: good use, dangerous drugs and self-medication
lessons.objective: Classify drugs, detect dangerous drugs and question self-medication.
lessons.course:
Medicines (drugs) treat illnesses when a health worker prescribes them. Dangerous drugs harm the body and the mind: tobacco, alcohol for children, cannabis, “tramadol” taken without prescription, street drugs.
Self-medication means taking medicine without advice. It is dangerous: wrong medicine, wrong dose, fake medicines sold in the street, hidden illness. We take medicine only with an adult and a health worker’s advice, we follow the dose and we keep medicines out of reach of small children.
lessons.model: The adult reads a medicine box with the child: name, dose, expiry date, and explains why we do not buy medicines in the street.
lessons.guided: Sort situations into safe and unsafe. Role play: a friend offers you pills; you say no and tell an adult.
lessons.exercise: Who should advise us before we take a medicine?
lessons.remediation: Learn one rule: no medicine without an adult and a health worker.
lessons.transfer: Help an adult put medicines out of reach of small children.

practice.prompt: A friend offers you pills to “feel strong”. What do you do?
choices: say no and tell a trusted adult
practice.answer: say no and tell a trusted adult
practice.explanation: Unknown pills can be very dangerous.

practice.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Read the box with an adult.

practice.prompt: Why are street medicines dangerous?
practice.answer: They may be fake or badly kept.

lessons.title: Lire un texte : chez le médecin
lessons.objective: Lire à haute voix un texte de six phrases, trouver l’idée générale et répondre à des questions.
lessons.course: Pour comprendre un texte : lis le titre, lis le texte une fois en entier, puis cherche qui, où, quand, quoi. L’idée générale dit en une phrase de quoi parle le texte.

support.title: Lis le texte
support.text:
Chez le médecin
Ce matin, Bih a de la fièvre et elle tousse. Sa mère l’emmène au centre de santé. Le médecin écoute sa respiration et regarde sa gorge. Il dit que Bih a une angine. Il lui donne un médicament à prendre trois fois par jour. Bih doit aussi boire beaucoup d’eau et se reposer.

lessons.model: L’adulte lit le texte, puis dit l’idée générale : « Bih est malade et va chez le médecin. »
lessons.guided: Lis le texte à haute voix. Réponds aux questions. Dis l’idée générale en une phrase.
lessons.exercise: Combien de fois par jour Bih prend-elle son médicament ?
lessons.remediation: Lis une phrase, puis pose une question sur cette phrase.
lessons.transfer: Lis le texte à ta famille et explique-le en anglais.

practice.prompt: Quelle est l’idée générale du texte ?
choices: Bih est malade et va chez le médecin.
practice.answer: Bih est malade et va chez le médecin.
practice.explanation: Le texte parle de la visite au médecin.

practice.prompt: Remets les phrases dans l’ordre du texte.
items: Sa mère l’emmène au centre de santé.

practice.prompt: Écoute le texte.
practice.listen: Ce matin, Bih a de la fièvre et elle tousse. Sa mère l’emmène au centre de santé. Le médecin écoute sa respiration et regarde sa gorge.

lessons.title: Rights of children and women
lessons.objective: Identify the rights of children and women, explain the duties that go with them and denounce acts of abuse.
lessons.course:
Every person has human rights: life, dignity, health, education, protection, freedom of expression. Children have the right to go to school, to be protected from violence, early marriage and hard labour. Women have the same rights as men: to study, work, own property, vote and be safe.
We all have duties: respect others’ rights. If a child or a woman is abused, tell a trusted adult, the head teacher, a social worker or the police.
lessons.model: The teacher reads a story: a girl kept at home to sell in the market; her neighbour talks to the parents and she goes back to school.
lessons.guided: Make two lists: rights of children, rights of women. Act a scene where a pupil reports a problem to a trusted adult.
lessons.exercise: Name one right of every child.
lessons.answer: For example: the right to go to school.
lessons.remediation: Start with three rights: school, health, protection.
lessons.transfer: Talk with your family about equal rights for girls and boys at home.

practice.prompt: Which situation respects children’s rights?
choices: a girl and a boy both go to school
a child works all day in a quarry
a child is beaten every day
practice.answer: a girl and a boy both go to school
practice.explanation: All children have the right to education.

practice.prompt: Match each right with an example.
practice.answer: education: school; health: vaccination; protection: no violence.

practice.prompt: To whom can you report abuse?
practice.answer: For example: a trusted adult or the head teacher.

lessons.title: Laying the table and meals for different people
lessons.objective: Lay the table appropriately, differentiate meals for different people and show good table manners.
lessons.course:
To lay the table: a clean cloth or mat, the plate in the middle, the fork on the left, the knife on the right (blade towards the plate), the spoon on the right of the knife, the glass above the knife.
Meals differ: a baby needs soft food (pap, mashed food); a sick person needs light food and plenty of water; a worker needs energy foods; everyone needs a balanced diet.
Table manners: wash hands, wait for everyone, chew with the mouth closed, say thank you.
lessons.model: The adult lays one place at the table and names each item and its position.
lessons.guided: Lay the table for four people. Plan a meal for a baby, a sick person and a farmer.
lessons.exercise: On which side do we put the fork?
lessons.remediation: Remember: fork and left both have four letters.
lessons.transfer: Lay the table for your family this week.

practice.prompt: Match each person with a suitable meal.
pairs: energy food like plantains and beans
practice.answer: baby: pap; sick person: light soup; farmer: energy food.

practice.prompt: Where is the glass placed?
practice.explanation: The glass is above the knife.

practice.prompt: Draw one place laid on the table.
practice.answer: A plate with fork, knife, spoon and glass.
practice.explanation: Fork left, knife and spoon right.

lessons.title: Painting a health poster
lessons.objective: Paint an artwork using appropriate colour combinations to send a clear message.
lessons.course:
Colours can work together. Complementary colours make each other stronger: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) attract attention; cool colours (blue, green) calm.
A poster needs a short message in big letters, a clear picture and strong contrasts so that people read it from far.
lessons.model: The adult sketches a poster “Wash your hands!” with dark blue letters on a yellow background and a picture of hands.
lessons.guided: Paint a poster on a health message (hand washing, mosquito nets, clean water). Use two complementary colours.
lessons.exercise: Which colour is complementary to red?
lessons.remediation: Use a colour wheel to find opposite colours.
lessons.transfer: Display your poster at home or at school.
lessons.materials: Paints or crayons, large paper, a colour wheel.

practice.prompt: Match each colour with its complementary colour.
practice.explanation: Complementary colours are opposite on the wheel.

practice.prompt: Which poster is easiest to read from far?
choices: big dark letters on a light background
practice.answer: big dark letters on a light background

practice.prompt: Paint or draw your health poster.
practice.answer: A poster with a short message and a picture.

lessons.title: The cartwheel, step by step
lessons.objective: Use different postures to keep stability and move using hands and legs: the cartwheel.
lessons.course:
Cartwheel: stand facing forward, arms up; step forward with one leg, place one hand then the other on the ground in a line, kick the legs over one after the other, land one foot then the other, arms up.
Practise on soft ground with an adult, first with bent legs, then straighter. One child at a time.
lessons.model: The adult draws a line and hand marks on the ground and shows a slow cartwheel.
lessons.guided: Practise “bunny hops” sideways over a line, then a low cartwheel with an adult nearby.
lessons.exercise: What do we place on the ground first: the hands or the feet?
lessons.remediation: Practise putting the hands on the line and kicking the legs up a little.
lessons.transfer: Show the safety rules of gymnastics to your family.

practice.prompt: Put the cartwheel in order.

choices: on soft ground with an adult
practice.answer: on soft ground with an adult

practice.prompt: How many children practise at a time?

lessons.title: Entertaining with a tale: the art of eloquence
lessons.objective: Narrate a tale with eloquence to entertain people and draw its lesson.
lessons.course: A good storyteller uses a traditional opening that asks for attention, changes the voice for each character, uses gestures, asks the audience to answer (call and response), keeps the events in order and ends with the lesson.

support.title: A short original tale
support.text: Hare boasted that he was the fastest animal and laughed at Snail. Snail said: “Let us race to the river.” Hare ran and stopped to sleep under a tree. Snail kept moving, slowly but without stopping. When Hare woke up, Snail was already drinking at the river. All the animals laughed at Hare.

lessons.model: The adult tells the tale with different voices and asks the listeners: “Who will win?”
lessons.guided: Retell the tale with eloquence. Then ask an elder for a tale in the family language and tell it to the class.
lessons.exercise: What is the lesson of the tale?
lessons.answer: For example: slow and steady wins; do not boast.
lessons.remediation: Retell with three pictures: the boast, the race, the end.
lessons.transfer: Tell a tale at a family gathering.

practice.prompt: Put the events in order.
What helps a storyteller entertain?
Listen to the tale.
practice.listen: Hare boasted that he was the fastest animal and laughed at Snail. Snail said: let us race to the river. Hare ran and stopped to sleep under a tree. Snail kept moving, slowly but without stopping.

lessons.title: Sitting well in front of a screen
lessons.objective: Adopt a good sitting position, position the screen and keyboard properly and prevent health problems.
lessons.course:
Good posture: sit straight with the back supported, feet flat on the floor, the top of the screen at eye level and an arm’s length away, the keyboard close with wrists straight.
Problems from bad habits: back and neck pain, tired or dry eyes, sore wrists. Rule of 20: every 20 minutes, look at something far away for 20 seconds; take breaks and move.
lessons.model: The adult shows a bad posture (bent, too close) and a good posture, and adjusts the screen.
lessons.guided: Check the posture of a partner with a checklist of five points. Make a poster of good habits.
lessons.exercise: How far should the screen be from your eyes?
lessons.remediation: Learn three points: back straight, feet flat, screen far enough.
lessons.transfer: Check how your family members sit in front of phones or TV.
lessons.materials: A chair, a table, a checklist.

practice.prompt: Match each problem with a prevention.
pairs: sit straight with the back supported

practice.prompt: Where should the top of the screen be?
